entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.1">1Ch 15:1</reference> <div eID="gen5735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5736" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.12">2Sa 6:12</reference> the whole matter is introduced by a statement that the motive which had determined the king to bring the ark to Jerusalem, was his having heard of the blessing which the ark had brought upon the house of Obed-edom. In our narrative (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.1">1Ch 15:1</reference>), the remark that David, while building his house in Jerusalem, prepared a place for the ark of God, and erected a tent for it, forms the transition from the account of his palace-building (1Ch 14:1.) to the bringing in of the ark. The words, “he made unto himself houses,” do not denote, as Bertheau thinks, the building of other houses besides the palaces built with the help of King Hiram (<reference osisRef="1Chr.14.1">1Ch 14:1</reference>). For עשׂה is not synonymous with בּנה, but expresses the preparation of the building for a dwelling, and the words refer to the completion of the palace as a dwelling-place for the king and his wives and children. In thus making the palace which had been built fit for a habitation, David prepared a place for the ark, which, together with its tent, was to be placed in his palace. As to the reasons which influenced David in determining to erect a new tabernacle for the ark, instead of causing the old and sacred tabernacle to be brought from Gibeon to Jerusalem for the purpose, see the remarks introductory to 2 Sam 6.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.2-1Chr.15.3">1Ch 15:2-3</reference> <div eID="gen5736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5737" type="x-p"/> The reason for the preparations made on this occasion for the solemn progress is assigned in the statement that David had resolved to cause the ark to be carried by the Levites alone, because God had chosen them thereto; cf. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.4-1Chr.15.10">1Ch 15:4-10</reference> <div eID="gen5737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5738" type="x-p"/> From among assembled Israel David then specially gathered together the heads of the priests and Levites, to determine upon the details of this solemn procession. “The sons of Aaron” are the high priests Zadok and Abiathar, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.11">1Ch 15:11</reference>; and the “Levites” are the six princes named in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.5-1Chr.15.10">1Ch 15:5-10</reference>, with their brethren, viz., (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.5-1Chr.15.7">1Ch 15:5-7</reference>) the three heads of the families into which the tribe of Levi was divided, and which corresponded to the three sons of Levi, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, respectively (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.16">Exo 6:16</reference>): Uriel head of the Kohathites, Asaiah of the Merarites, and Joel head of the Gershonites, with their brethren. Kohath is first enumerated, because Aaron the chief of the priests was descended from Kohath, and because to the Kohathites there fell, on account of their nearer relationship to the priests, the duty of serving in that which is most holy, the bearing of the holiest vessels of the tabernacle. See Num 4:4, Num 4:15; Num 7:9; as to Uriel, see on Num 6:24; for Asaiah, see 6:30; and as to Joel, see 1Ch 6:33. Then in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.8">1Ch 15:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.9">1Ch 15:9</reference> we have the heads of three other Kohathite families: Shemaiah, chief of the sons of Elizaphan, i.e., Elizaphan son of the Kohathite Uzziel (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.22">Exo 6:22</reference>); Eliel, chief of the sons of Hebron the Kohathite (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.18">Exo 6:18</reference>); and Amminadab, chief of the sons of Uzziel. The sons of Uzziel, consequently, were divided into two fathers'-houses: the one founded by Uzziel’s son Elizaphan, and named after him (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.8">1Ch 15:8</reference>); the other founded by his other sons, and called by his name. Of the fathers'-houses here enumerated, four belong to Kohath, and one each to Merari and Gershon; and the Kohathites were called to take part in the solemn act in greater numbers than the Merarites and Gershonites, since the transport of the ark was the Kohathites’ special duty.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.11-1Chr.15.12">1Ch 15:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen5738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5739" type="x-p"/> Zadok of the line of Eleazar (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.1-1Chr.6.15">1Ch 6:1-15</reference>), and Abiathar of the line of Ithamar, were the heads of the two priestly lines, and at that time both held the office of high priest (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.3">1Ch 24:3</reference>; cf. 2Sa 15:24., <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.25">2Sa 20:25</reference>). entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.13">1Ch 15:13</reference> “For because in the beginning (i.e., when the ark was removed from the house of Amminadab, <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.1-1Chr.13.14">1Ch 13:1-14</reference>) it was not you (sc., who brought it up), did Jahve our God made a breach upon us,” sc. by the slaying of Uzza, 1Ch 13:11. In the first clause the predicate is wanting, but it may easily be supplied from the context. The contracted form למבּרשׁונה, made up of למה and בּראשׁונה, is unique, since מה is so united only with small words, as in מזּה, <reference osisRef="Exod.4.2">Exo 4:2</reference>, מלּכם, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.15">Isa 3:15</reference>; but we find מתּלאה for מה־תּלאה, Mal 1:13; cf. Ew. §91, <hi type="italic">d</hi>. למה here signifies: on account of this which = because; cf.'Ew. §222, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, and 353, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. “This was done, because we did not seek Him according to the right,” which required that the ark, upon which Jehovah sits enthroned, should be carried by Levites, and touched by no unholy person, or one who is not a priest (Num 4:15).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.16-1Chr.15.18">1Ch 15:16-18</reference> <div eID="gen5740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5741" type="x-p"/> David gave the princes of the Levites a further charge to appoint singers with musical instruments for the solemn procession, which they accordingly did. שׁיר כּלי, instruments to accompany the song. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.16">1Ch 15:16</reference> three kinds of these are named: נבלים, <hi type="italic">nablia</hi>, ψαλτήρια, which Luther has translated by psalter, corresponds to the Arabic santir, which is an oblong box with a broad bottom and a somewhat convex sounding-board, over which strings of wire are stretched; an instrument something like the <hi type="italic">cithara</hi>. כּנּרות, harps, more properly lutes, as this instrument more resembled our lute than the harp, and corresponded to the Arabic catgut instrument <hi type="italic">el ‛ûd</hi> (<hi type="italic">l - c ûd</hi>); cf. Wetzstein in Delitzsch, <hi type="italic">Isaiah</hi>, S. 702, der 2 Aufl., where, however, the statement that the santir is essentially the same as the old German cymbal, <hi type="italic">vulgo</hi> Hackebrett, is incorrect, and calculated to bring confusion into the matter, for the cymbal was an instrument provided with a small bell. מצלתּים, the later word for צלצלים, cymbals, castanets; see on 2Sa 6:5. משׁמיעים does not belong to the three before-mentioned instruments (Berth.), but, as is clear from <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19">1Ch 15:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.28">1Ch 15:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.5">1Ch 16:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.42">1Ch 16:42</reference>, undoubtedly only to מצלתּים (Böttcher, <hi type="italic">Neue krit. Aehrenlese</hi>, iii. S. 223); but the meaning is not “modulating,” but “sounding clear or loud,” - according to the proper meaning of the word, to make to hear. The infinitive clause וגו להרים belongs to the preceding sentence: “in order to heighten the sound (both of the song and of the instrumental music) to joy,” i.e., to the expression of joy. לשׂימחה is frequently used to express festive joy: cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.25">1Ch 15:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.23.18">2Ch 23:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.30">2Ch 29:30</reference>; but also as early as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.12">2Sa 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6">1Sa 18:6</reference>; Jdg 16:23, etc. - In <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.17">1Ch 15:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.18">1Ch 15:18</reference> the names of the singers and players are introduced; then in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19-1Chr.15.21">1Ch 15:19-21</reference> they are named in connection with the instruments they played; and finally, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.22-1Chr.15.24">1Ch 15:22-24</reference>, the other Levites and priests who took part in the celebration are mentioned. The three chief singers, the Kohathite Heman, the Gershonite Asaph, and the Merarite Ethan, form the first class. See on <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.33">1Ch 6:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.39">1Ch 6:39</reference>, and 1Ch 6:44. To the second class (המּשׁנים, cf. המּשׁנה, 2Ki 23:4) belonged thirteen or fourteen persons, for in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.21">1Ch 15:21</reference> an Azaziah is named in the last series who is omitted in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.18">1Ch 15:18</reference>; and it is more probable that his name has been dropped out of <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.18">1Ch 15:18</reference> than that it came into our text, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.21">1Ch 15:21</reference>, by an error. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.18">1Ch 15:18</reference> בּן comes in after זכריהוּ by an error or transcription, as we learn from the w before the following name, and from a comparison of <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.20">1Ch 15:20</reference> and 1Ch 15:25. The name יעזיאל is in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.20">1Ch 15:20</reference> written עזיאל, <hi type="italic">Yodh</hi> being rejected; and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.5">1Ch 16:5</reference> it is יעיאל, which is probably only a transcriber’s error, since יעיאל occurs along with it both in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.18">1Ch 15:18</reference> and in 1Ch 16:5. The names Benaiah and Maaseiah, which are repeated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.20">1Ch 15:20</reference>, have been there transposed. All the other names in vv.18 and 20 coincide.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19-1Chr.15.21">1Ch 15:19-21</reference> <div eID="gen5741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5742" type="x-p"/> These singers formed three choirs, according to the instruments they played. Heman, Asaph, and Ethan played brazen cymbals להשׁמיע (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19">1Ch 15:19</reference>); Benaiah and the seven who follow played <hi type="italic">nablia</hi> (<hi type="italic">psalteria</hi>) עלמות על (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.20">1Ch 15:20</reference>); while the last six played lutes (harps) לנצּח השּׁמינית על (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.21">1Ch 15:21</reference>). These three Hebrew words plainly denote different keys in singing, but are, owing to our small acquaintance with the music of the Hebrews, obscure, and cannot be interpreted with certainty. נצּח, going over from the fundamental signification glitter, shine, into the idea of outshining and superior capacity, overwhelming ability, might also, as a musical term, denote the conducting of the playing and singing as well as the leading of them. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.22-1Chr.15.24">1Ch 15:22-24</reference> “Chenaniah, the prince of the Levites, for the bearing, teacher in bearing; for he was instructed in it.” Since Chenaniah does not occur among the six princes of the Levites in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.5-1Chr.15.10">1Ch 15:5-10</reference>, and is called in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.27">1Ch 15:27</reference> המּשּׂא השׂר, we must here also join בּמשּׂא (as most editions punctuate the first במשׂא, while according to Norzi בּמּשּׂא is the right reading even in the first case) closely with שׂר־הלויּם, with the meaning that Chenaniah was captain of the Levites who had charge of the bearing of the ark, a chief of the Levites who bore it. The word משּׂא is,however, very variously interpreted. The lxx have ἄρχων τῶν ᾠδῶν, and the Vulgate, <hi type="italic">prophetiae praeerat ad praecinendam melodiam;</hi> whence Luther translates: the master in song to teach them to sing. This translation cannot, however, be linguistically upheld; the word משּׂא means only the bearing of the burden (Num 4:19, Num 4:27, etc.; <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.3">2Ch 35:3</reference>), and a prophetical utterance of an oppressive or threatening character (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.1">Isa 13:1</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">Isa 15:1</reference>, etc.). But from this second signification neither the general meaning prophetia, nor, if we wish to go back upon the קול נשׂא, to raise the voice, the signification master of song, <hi type="italic">supremus musicus</hi> (Lavat.), <hi type="italic">or qui principatum tenebat in cantu illo sublimiore</hi> (Vatabl.), can be derived. The meaning <hi type="italic">prophetia</hi>, moreover, does not suit the context, and we must consequently, with Bertheau and others, hold fast the signification of bearing. We are determined in favour of this, (1) by the context, which here treats of the bearing of the ark, for which משּׂא is the usual word; and (2) by the circumstance that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.29">1Ch 26:29</reference> Chenaniah is mentioned as the chief of the Levites for the external business, which goes to show, if the persons are identical, that he here had the oversight of the external business of the transport. יסר is not the inf. absol., which cannot stand directly for the <hi type="italic">verb. finit.</hi>; nor is it the imperf. of סרר in the signification of שׂרר (Bertheau and others), but a nominal formation from יסר (cf. on this formation as the most proper designation of the actor, Ew. §152, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), in the signification teacher, which is shown by <reference osisRef="Isa.28.26">Isa 28:26</reference> certainly to belong to יסר. The clause בּמּשּׂא יסר gives the explanation of the preceding בּמשּׂא, or it specifies what Chenaniah had to do in the procession. He had to take the lead in the bearing because he was מבין in it, i.e., was instructed in that which was to be observed in it. - In <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.23">1Ch 15:23</reference> two doorkeepers for the ark are named; and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.24">1Ch 15:24</reference>, at the end of the enumeration of the Levites who were busied about the transport, two additional names are mentioned as those of men who had the same duty. The business of these doorkeepers was, as Seb. Schmidt has already remarked on 2 Sam 6, <, <hi type="italic">non tam introitum aperire arcae, quam custodire, ne ad eam irrumperetur</hi>. Between these two pairs of doorkeepers in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.24">1Ch 15:24</reference>, the priests, seven in number, who blew the trumpets, are named. The Kethibh מחצצרים is to be read מחצצרים, a denom. from חצצרה; the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> מחצרים is Hiph. of חצר, as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.6">2Ch 7:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.14">2Ch 13:14</reference>, and 2Ch 29:28. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.12">2Ch 5:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.13">2Ch 5:13</reference>, on the contrary, מחצּרים is partic. Pi. The blowing of the silver trumpets by the priests in this solemn procession rests on the prescription in Num 10:1-10, which see. The place assigned to these trumpet-blowing priests was either immediately before the ark, like the priestly trumpeters in the march round Jericho (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.4">Jos 6:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.6">Jos 6:6</reference>), or immediately after it. For, that these priests entered in the immediate vicinity of the ark, may be inferred from the fact that before and behind them were doorkeepers of the ark. The procession, then, was probably arranged in this way: (1) the singers and players in front, in three division; (2) Chenaniah, the captain of the bearers; (3) two doorkeepers; (4) the priests with the trumpets immediately before or after the ark; (5) two doorkeepers; (6) the king with the elders and captains of thousands (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.25">1Ch 15:25</reference>). The two doorkeepers Obededom and Jehiah (יחיּה), Rashi, Berth.,and others consider to be the same persons as the singers Obededom and Jeiel (יעיאל), supposing that the latter name is wrongly written in one of the passages. This, however, is incorrect, for the identity of the name Obededom is no sufficient ground for supposing the persons to be the same, since in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.38">1Ch 16:38</reference> the singer Obededom and the doorkeeper Obededom the son of Jeduthun seem to be distinguished.
